newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaire rebels said protecting threatened gorillas.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels said protecting threatened gorillas.

text.p: Rebels now controlling almost half of Zaire have taken time out to ensure protection of threatened mountain gorillas in the east of the country, a leading expert on the animals said on Wednesday.

Elizabeth Kemf of the Geneva-based World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) told Reuters security of the gorillas, of whom only some 620 survive in the wild, had improved since the insurgents seized the eastern border region late last year.

"With the help of WWF emergency funds, they have been restoring the infrastructure and equipment of the Virunga National Park where many of the gorillas live, and retraining the park staff," she said.
"Prospects for the gorillas are looking a lot better than they were."

Kemf was speaking in advance of a new WWF report on the growing threat to the world's few remaining species of the great apes -- man's closest relative among the animals -- as human habitation and hunting reduce their habitat in Africa and Asia.
Mountain gorillas, made famous by American naturalist Dian Fossey and a hit film about her work with them in the region, live only in Virunga and forest areas across the border in Rwanda and Uganda.

The around 200 gorillas in the park in eastern Zaire had appeared increasingly threatened over the past three years as some 700,000 Hutu refugees from Rwanda camped in the area, destroying large areas of forest.
Wildlife officials believe refugees, and elements of the Zairean army, had also hunted the animals for meat. At least four were killed in 1995, they say.
But when the Tutsi-dominated rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces swept through last November, most of the refugees there returned home and Zairean army units fled or switched sides.

Earlier this year, a WWF official in the region said the rebels -- whose leader Laurent Kabila says he aims to oust Zaire's beleaguered President Mobutu Sese Seko -- recognised the benefits of conservation.
A new governor appointed by Kabila was doing his best to protect the park, the official said.
